Lessons.Title: Angles, Arcs, and Radii
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Use similarity of circles to show arc-length divided by radius depends only on central angle, anticipating radians.
For equal central angle, L/r is invariant across circles Both L and r scale equally

When two circles are scaled copies and their central angles match, corresponding arc lengths and radii scale by the same factor, so the quotient of arc length to radius is unchanged. This proportional relationship is the focus here; the new angular unit is introduced in the following lesson.

Authentic task: Draw two similar circles and compare same-angle arcs with explicit proportional proof; teacher scores. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct circle or radian model, valid assumptions, exact calculations/angle interpretation, and well-supported explanation. Diagrams and reasoning require teacher scoring.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 7 Lesson 10, CC BY 4.0. Independently written examples; no copied art or restricted assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Arc/radius ratio
KeyConcepts.Definition: For equal central angle, L/r is invariant across circles
KeyConcepts.Rule: Both L and r scale equally

KeyConcepts.Title: Angle dependence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Central angle θ degrees yields L/r=πθ/180

KeyConcepts.Title: Unitless quantity
KeyConcepts.Definition: When an arc length and its radius use identical linear units, their quotient is a dimensionless number; equal central angles yield equal quotients in similar circles.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compute s/r without naming a new angular unit yet; the next lesson introduces a new way to measure angles.
KeyConcepts.Example: For arc s=3 cm and radius r=2 cm, s/r=1.5, regardless of the circle's physical size.

Lessons.Title: Radian Sense
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Convert between degrees and radians and estimate meaningful quarter, half and full turns without confusing scale.
θrad=θdeg·π/180 θdeg=θrad·180/π
Quarter turn π/2; half turn π; full turn 2π Check angle placement on diagram Use exact expressions before approximation

The first-edition task emphasizes intuitive relative angle sizes, double number lines, and shading sectors in a pie-colouring challenge before formal degree–radian algorithms. Students must locate half-, quarter-, and other fractional turns on a circle and explain how angle and arc fraction correspond; exact conversions support but must not replace that geometric reasoning.

Authentic task: Annotate exact benchmark radian angles around unit circle; teacher reviews drawing. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct circle or radian model, valid assumptions, exact calculations/angle interpretation, and well-supported explanation. Diagrams and reasoning require teacher scoring.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 7 Lesson 12, CC BY 4.0. Independently written examples; no copied art or restricted assessment.

WorkedExamples.Title: Radian Sense: benchmark a pie sector with a double number line
WorkedExamples.Question: An angle has measure 5π/6 radians. Draw its sector on a circle, mark how much of a full turn it covers, and give the corresponding degree benchmark.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use 2π radians per full turn to locate sector fraction, then use known degree benchmarks.
Steps: Relative fraction of a full turn is (5π/6)/(2π)=5/12, which is less than a half-turn.
On a double number line mark 0 ↔ 0°, π/2 ↔ 90°, 5π/6 ↔ 150°, and π ↔ 180°; 5π/6 falls between π/2 and π.
Shade 5/12 of the circle from the chosen initial ray in the specified counterclockwise direction and label 150°.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 5π/6 radians equals 150°, covering 5/12 of a full circle.
WorkedExamples.Check: Counterclockwise shaded arc is smaller than a semicircle and greater than a quarter-circle; a teacher must verify the original sector drawing.

Lessons.Title: Using Radians
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Derive s=rθ and A=(1/2)r²θ for a circular sector whose central angle θ is in radians.
s=rθ with θ in radians and r>0 Based on definition θ=s/r
A=(1/2)r²θ for 0≤θ≤2π, measured in radians Use area fraction θ/(2π) Use θ/(2π) for sector fraction

First-edition source task alignment: learners use a table of radii and circular arc lengths and graph their ordered pairs. For a fixed central angle, arc length is proportional to radius and the graph's slope is the radian measure θ, in s=rθ. This coordinate-graph argument and interpretation of slope must accompany, not be replaced by, sector-area formula drills.

Authentic task: Students derive sector formula from area fraction then construct three sectors; teacher reviews derivation. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct circle or radian model, valid assumptions, exact calculations/angle interpretation, and well-supported explanation. Diagrams and reasoning require teacher scoring.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 7 Lesson 13, CC BY 4.0. Independently written examples; no copied art or restricted assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Arc formula
KeyConcepts.Definition: s=rθ with θ in radians and r>0

KeyConcepts.Title: Sector formula
KeyConcepts.Definition: A=(1/2)r²θ for 0≤θ≤2π, measured in radians

KeyConcepts.Title: Arc-length line and slope
KeyConcepts.Definition: For the same central angle θ, arc length s is a linear function of radius r: s=θr, with r≥0 and θ measured in radians.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Plot (r,s) and divide vertical change by horizontal change. The line passes through (0,0), and slope Δs/Δr=θ; both s and r use the same length units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Using Radians — interpret a radius/arc-length graph
WorkedExamples.Question: An original circular-path design records radius r (m) and arc length s (m) as (2,3),(6,9),(11,16.5),(14,21). Make a table and graph; determine the line's slope, interpret the common angle, and predict the arc for radius 20 m.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the proportional graph s=θr and verify constant ratios at each measured pair.
Steps: Calculate s/r for each positive radius: 3/2=9/6=16.5/11=21/14=1.5, so all ordered pairs belong to a line through the origin.
Plot (r,s) with radius on the horizontal axis and arc length on the vertical axis. The slope is (9−3)/(6−2)=6/4=1.5, equal to θ in radians.
Use s=1.5r for r=20 m to predict an arc length of 30 m; both axes and the slope interpretation must be labelled.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Line s=1.5r; slope and central angle are 1.5 radians; at radius 20 m, arc length 30 m.
WorkedExamples.Check: Four input pairs each have s/r=1.5, including (14,21). Radius and arc must have consistent units; 1.5 radians is dimensionless.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using θ=90 directly in radian formula
Using r instead of r² for area

SummaryPoints: Derive s=rθ and A=(1/2)r²θ for a circular sector whose central angle θ is in radians.
On the arc-length versus radius graph for a fixed central angle, slope equals angle θ in radians: s=θr; sector area then follows A=(1/2)r²θ.

Opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral sum 180° Check all vertices on circle

At tangency radius perpendicular Use Pythagoras in right triangle from external point s=rθ and A=1/2r²θ

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare sector-area pizza offers
WorkedExamples.Question: Offer A is a 60° slice of radius-6 pizza priced 3 units; B a 40° slice of radius-9 pizza priced 4 units. Which is cheaper per square unit?
WorkedExamples.Method: Find exact sector area then compare price divided by area.
Steps: A has area (60/360)π·6²=6π, so price per area=3/(6π)=1/(2π).
B has area (40/360)π·9²=9π, so price per area=4/(9π).
Compare 1/2 with 4/9: since 4/9<1/2, offer B has smaller price per unit area.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Offer B is cheaper per area (4/(9π) versus 1/(2π)).
WorkedExamples.Check: Assumes equal material quality and comparable slice geometry; area is square units.
